outline.chapter_title: Introduction: The Limits of Tokenization and the Rise of Byte-Level Modeling
outline.description: This chapter introduces the fundamental problem of fixed-vocabulary tokenization in Large Language Models (LLMs), highlighting its inefficiencies and biases. It presents the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) as a novel architecture that operates directly on raw bytes, offering a path to improved efficiency, robustness, and scalability.
subtopics: The role and limitations of tokenization in modern LLMs
Biases introduced by static vocabularies: domain sensitivity, noise vulnerability, and multilingual inequity
The computational cost of byte-level models: why previous attempts failed at scale
Introduction to the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT): Core philosophy and contributions
Overview of dynamic compute allocation vs. static token processing

outline.chapter_title: Dynamic Patching Strategies: From Bytes to Latent Units
outline.description: This chapter details the mechanism by which BLT groups raw bytes into 'patches' rather than fixed tokens. It explores various patching strategies, culminating in the entropy-based dynamic patching method that allows the model to adapt its computational granularity based on data complexity.
subtopics: Defining patches vs. tokens: The concept of variable-length units without a fixed vocabulary
Static patching methods: Strided (fixed K) and Space-based patching
Limitations of rule-based heuristics in diverse domains and languages
Entropy-based patching: Using next-byte prediction uncertainty to define boundaries
Global threshold vs. Approximate Monotonic constraints for boundary detection
Incremental patching: Ensuring autoregressive generation without future context

outline.chapter_title: The BLT Architecture: A Hierarchical Transformer Design
outline.description: This chapter provides a deep dive into the three-component architecture of BLT: the Local Encoder, the Global Latent Transformer, and the Local Decoder. It explains how these components interact to process byte sequences efficiently while maintaining high representational power.
subtopics: High-level overview: The flow from bytes to patches and back to bytes
The Local Encoder ($\mathcal{E}$): Mapping bytes to patch representations with lightweight transformers
Hash n-gram embeddings: Enhancing local context awareness without large vocabularies
Cross-attention mechanisms: Pooling byte representations into latent patches (Encoder)
The Global Latent Transformer ($\mathcal{G}$): The heavy-lifting autoregressive model operating on patches
The Local Decoder ($\mathcal{D}$): Expanding patch representations back into raw byte sequences
Decoder cross-attention: Generating byte sequences conditioned on global context

outline.description: This chapter analyzes the computational efficiency of BLT compared to token-based models. It covers the methodology for calculating FLOPs in a byte-level context, presents scaling trends across different model sizes, and demonstrates how BLT achieves better performance under fixed inference budgets.
subtopics: FLOPs estimation for byte-level architectures vs. token-based architectures
Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) as a tokenizer-independent metric for performance evaluation
Compute-optimal scaling trends: Matching Llama 3 performance with fewer FLOPs
The trade-off between patch size and model size under fixed inference budgets
'Patches Scale Better Than Tokens': Evidence from fixed-inference scaling experiments
Data efficiency: Training on 4T bytes with 8B parameters
